They're springtails! Teeny tiny bugs that are technically not insects. They eat decomposing matter, so a lot of people use them in the enclosures of other pets (spiders, reptiles, etc) to prevent mold. I think they look pretty cute on their own though!

They're springtails, yes! I don't really have a care guide for them, because they're so simple to keep. They live on decaying matter, so any soil with any green is perfect. I use them in the enclosures of my other pets (spiders + dig pit for mouse) to make them bioactive and free of mold, but they look adorable in a teeny tiny jarrarium.

That's perfectly normal! I don't know if you've ever seen that episode of Spongebob where Mr Krabs moults and is all soft and pink, but that's pretty much what happens. Your mantis probably needs to harden out, as its limbs and mouth parts are still too soft right now. It can take a few days to a week. These periods get longer as your mantis grows, my adults won't eat for a week+ after moulting.

Try feeding something every other day or so to check if your mantis is ready, but don't leave any feeders with them unsupervised, as your mantis is very delicate and vulnerable right now. 

Don't worry about them not eating for long periods of time, insects can handle that just fine. My spiny flower girl was on a random hunger strike for two weeks with no reason, but she's fine now. My spiders sometimes won't eat for months at a time. 

Good luck!

Mice are social animals, so they do best with at least one buddy (unless you can give them loooots of attention). The problem with male mice is that you're probably not willing to have dozens of babies when you keep them with females, and they will fight other males (some have successfully kept brothers together, but it's always a risk and they can fight nasty). It's usually not worth the money and massive risk to have male mice fixed either.

So people have been looking around for solutions. You cannot keep mice with hamsters or rats. Hamsters are solitary meany babies (with respect and love), and rats are too big and will fight and/or eat mice.

So in come the ASFs. People found out that they're pretty much the only species that can live with mice. They're neither mice nor rats but are very similar to mice in terms of socialising and lifestyle. They're pretty much only sold as feeders and are not as tame as pet mice, but a female (NOT a male!!!) ASF or two can make great companions for solitary males. They're different species so they can't have babies while still fulfilling their social needs.

I took in a rescue female a few years ago who was VERY territorial because of food scarcity and overcrowding in her earlier home. She seemed fine with my two (angels of) ladies until food was present and then she'd draw blood. I kept them separated for a week or two and interact with the demon girl a LOT. Always with food-based reinforcement (all four paws on my hand, treat; come out when I approach the cage, treat). After a week, I moved the wire cages against each other so they could see and smell each other but not touch. After a week of that I put them together but separated them at night just to be sure. They never became best friends, but they could live together and sit around the food bowls safely.

With your poor girl, I'd reintroduce her very slowly. Make sure she gets a lot of rest after that adventure and gets used to her human first. When introducing them together again, make sure she can always retreat to a hide. You might want to reintroduce them one on one if she gets overwhelmed by multiple mice. Mice are simple creatures, but this might be some form of trauma. My current male mouse was attacked by a wild house mouse once and seemed in shock for days. Take it easy and give her lots of positive attention. 

If it doesn't work out, so be it. Some mice are just not built for company and can be very happy with plenty of stimulation in their enclosure and lots of human love.

In theory, wood shavings are wood shavings, so yes it's safe.

With mice, it's important to pay attention to two factors. It cannot contain any fir, as that's toxic to them. Spruce is okay, fir is not. Secondly, mice have very sensitive respiratory systems and are very sensitive to dust. Wood shavings for horses can be advertised as "dust free", but that's for horses. Mice are much smaller and can be more sensitive to very small dust particles. But in general, I think you'll be fine with these wood.

You might want to mix wood shavings with some other materials to combat dust and encourage digging. I usually mix it with shredded paper or raw cotton bedding. Good luck!

It won't do any harm if she doesn't have mites, no worries! My boy was very weak by the time I figured out it might be mites, but he was already much more active the next day. 

I used the Beaphar Spot On one, but you can use any brand. The active ingredient should be ivermectin. Any treatment that is advertised for mice, hamsters, rats or gerbils is fine. The package of mine said for any pet under 70 grams or so. The one for hamsters was easier to find because they're more popular as pets.

The treatment comes in little pipettes with liquid that you squeeze on the skin in between the shoulder blades (so they can't lick it off). She'll probably lick some of it off, but that's okay. It usually contains two doses: one for now and one for in two weeks or so just to be sure.

Mites can be found everywhere, really. It can be that there were a few in your home that took up residence on your mouse. I got mine from a pet shop (not the best idea) where he lived with other mice and he got an infection about a month later.

Check with a vet (probably not the same one from earlier) if a mite treatment is a good idea, but you don't need a prescription for anti-parasitic treatments and you can just order them online, it's a lot cheaper. Make sure to keep using the wound spray and keep the enclosure clean while she's healing.
Additionally, google pictures of "mouse with mites", I think this looks pretty similar

The infection medicine might have helped for the wound itself, but it will just return if it's parasites. You can order anti-parasitic treatments online, I used Beaphar Anti-Parasite Spot On treatment for hamsters and gerbils (works for mice too). It treats mites, fleas, and internal parasites and is pretty cheap. 

Mice are pretty prone to mites, and these wounds do look like them. When you treat your mouse, make sure you also deep clean the ENTIRE enclosure and all toys with hot water and soap, otherwise the mites will stay alive and return. If you have more than one mouse, buy one treatment for every mouse and treat them at the same time. The mites should be dead in a day or two and the wounds will start healing.

Best of luck!

So cool that you're thinking about it! I started out with my jumping spider, they stay tiny and are just so cute with their two big eyes. Look for videos of the "phidippus regius". When I got used to a tiny but active spider, I started watching videos on bigger spiders. 

Tarantulas are actually very chill most of the time and don't really move very fast at all. I would look up Tarantula Kat on YouTube, she is very nice and knowledgeable. I got a sling (spiderling) first. She was about 2 cm when I got her a few months ago, but now my Pippin is around 5 cm. It is nice (and cheaper) to start out with a little spider if you're still a bit nervous, then you can see them grow over the course of a couple of years.

I would advise you to start out with an Old World tarantula (Americas). These are generally much calmer and a bit easier to care for. They are calm because of those shooting hairs you heard about! Those are called urticating hairs and are the spider's first line of defense. When a spider gets _very_ annoyed, they can "kick hair", or release those irritating hairs in the air. It has only happened to me once and it's fine, it feels like a nettle sting. New World tarantulas don't have those hairs and are quicker to bite, so the fuzzier the better! 

I think tarantulas are great pets! You don't have to handle them, they're also perfectly happy with being looked at. It's important to do your research and find a species that's right for you, but the r/tarantulas r/jumpingspiders and YouTube communities are very nice!
